segments.title: Which Coreopsis is under discussion?
segments.summary: The opening distinguishes HMS Coreopsis from the naval drifter Coreopsis II and tentatively identifies the submarine it helped sink off Scotland as UB-85.
segments.body: HMS Coreopsis should not be confused with the similarly named naval drifter Coreopsis II. The drifter worked with a destroyer in sinking a submarine off Scotland, tentatively identified as UB-85. The rest of the video concerns the Flower-class sloop and its varied career. This correction helps separate two small Royal Navy vessels with near-identical names.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes HMS Coreopsis from the similarly named drifter Coreopsis II and tentatively identifies the submarine sunk with a destroyer's involvement off Scotland as UB-85.

segments.title: Coreopsis as a concealed-armament Q-ship
segments.summary: Coreopsis served as a decoy warship with concealed guns, operating with the Grand Fleet, in the Mediterranean, and from Gibraltar under false names.
segments.body: Coreopsis is an outstanding example of a First World War Q-ship. Concealed armament allowed the vessel to appear harmless before engaging an enemy that approached. She served with the Grand Fleet and in the Mediterranean, then operated from Gibraltar under the false names Bursley and Biggo. She was sold for breaking up in 1922, after a wartime career that helped define the Royal Navy's later sloop concept.

evidence.note: The transcript describes concealed-armament decoy service, Grand Fleet and Mediterranean deployments, Gibraltar false names, and sale in 1922.

segments.title: A compact hull with useful carrying margin
segments.summary: Tonnage, displacement, dimensions, and draft show how a small sloop retained roughly 450 tons of useful carrying capacity.
segments.body: The stated tonnage and displacement figures leave roughly 450 tons for fuel, stores, armament, and other loads. Coreopsis measured 262 feet 3 inches overall with a 35-foot beam. Her fully laden draft could reach 13 feet 8 inches. The figures explain how a compact sloop retained enough carrying margin for several roles.

evidence.note: The transcript gives loaded and displacement tonnage, carrying difference, length, beam, and draft.

segments.title: Armament and endurance for a heavily armed small ship
segments.summary: A top speed of 16 knots, 260 tons of coal, QF 4-inch Mark IV guns, lighter guns, depth charges, and a complement of 92 show what the small hull carried.
segments.body: Coreopsis had a top speed of 16 knots and could carry 260 tons of coal. Her armament included two QF 4-inch Mark IV guns, two 12-pounder guns, depth charges, and sometimes 3-pounder guns. This combination made her heavily armed for such a small vessel. Operating the machinery and weapons required a complement of 92.

evidence.note: The transcript lists speed, coal, gun and depth-charge armament, and the complement.

segments.title: From Flower-class vessel to modern sloop concept
segments.summary: Coreopsis helps explain the First World War roots of the later Royal Navy sloop, even though the class was originally ordered for minesweeping rather than Q-ship duty.
segments.body: Coreopsis is an early example of the kind of sloop the Royal Navy developed after the First World War. Q-ship service was one possible use, but it was an adaptation rather than the class's original purpose. The Flower-class vessels were first ordered for minesweeping. A specialist minesweeping requirement produced ships that could later take on Q-ship and other duties.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the vessel an origin point for later sloops, notes Q-ship employment, and says the type was first ordered for minesweeping.

segments.title: Why peacetime small ships needed several roles
segments.summary: The overlap between sloops and minesweepers reflects operational utility and the political case needed to secure funding for small warships in peacetime.
segments.body: Through the 1910s, 1920s, and 1930s, sloops and minesweepers often met closely related needs. A small warship had to perform several duties instead of remaining tied to one task. Wartime construction could receive money quickly, whereas peacetime programmes needed a strong political justification. Minesweeping supplied a clear requirement, and a multi-purpose hull gave the navy broader value from the same procurement.

evidence.note: The transcript connects sloop-minesweeper overlap, multi-purpose capability, wartime funding, and the need to justify peacetime construction.
